castor.resume: Back in many European valleys. Discreet, active at dusk along the water.
identification: Trees gnawed into a sharpened-pencil shape at the water's edge
Wood chips, slides leading to the river
usages: Protected species: watch without disturbing, don't touch the dams.

aildesours.resume: Carpets of garlic-scented leaves in damp woodland in spring. Its look-alikes are among the most poisonous plants in our forests.
identification: Broad, soft, shiny leaves, each on its own thin stalk, coming straight out of the ground
Underside of the leaf matt, upper side shiny
White star-shaped flowers grouped in a ball (April–May)
Strong garlic smell when crushed — but the smell stays on your fingers: sniffing each leaf separately isn't enough

sosies.diff: Two or three leaves wrapped around each other on the same stalk, no garlic smell. Deadly.
Leaves in a tight tuft coming from the same point, stiffer, no smell. Deadly.
Arrow-shaped leaves with net-like veins, sometimes spotted with black.

usages: Pick leaf by leaf, never by the handful.
Raw in pesto or salad, or cooked like spinach.
If in doubt about a single leaf: throw everything away.

mure.resume: The easiest wild fruit: no dangerous look-alike in Belgium.
identification: Thorny bramble with long arching stems
Leaves with 3 or 5 toothed leaflets
Shiny black fruits made of small beads
usages: Raw. Pick from higher up rather than at ground level (see Fox).
Avoid roadsides.

framboise.resume: Common in forest clearings and felled areas.
identification: Upright stems with small, fine prickles
Whitish underside to the leaves
Hollow red fruit that comes away from its base
usages: Raw, wash it if picked low down.

myrtille.resume: Covers the ground in acid forests and heaths. Wild bilberries turn your mouth blue.
identification: Small shrub 20 to 50 cm tall with angular green stems
Small, oval, finely toothed leaves
Blue-black berries with a small crown at the top, purple flesh

sosies.diff: Round brown stems, bluish untoothed leaves, white flesh. Avoid in quantity.

usages: Raw. Wash or cook if picked at ground level (echinococcosis, see Fox).

fraise.resume: Tiny, very fragrant strawberries on forest edges and banks.
identification: Leaves with 3 toothed leaflets
White five-petalled flowers
Small conical red fruit, seeds on the surface

sosies.diff: Same look but a dry, non-fleshy fruit: harmless, just disappointing.

usages: Raw, wash it (grows at ground level).

sureau.resume: A hedgerow shrub. Fragrant flowers and rich berries, but raw berries and the leaves are poisonous.
identification: Shrub with grey, corky bark, white pith in the twigs
Wide, flat umbels of cream flowers in May–June
Hanging clusters of black berries in late summer

sosies.diff: A herbaceous plant that regrows each year (no wood), UPRIGHT berry clusters, unpleasant smell. Poisonous.
Red berries in oval clusters. Poisonous seeds: avoid.

usages: Flowers: in fritters or steeped in water (cordial).
Berries: always cooked, without green stalks (jam, syrup).
Never the leaves or bark.

oseille.resume: A sharp, lemony taste. Rich in oxalic acid: in small amounts.
identification: Arrow-shaped leaves, lobes at the base pointing downwards
Distinctly sour taste
Meadows and path edges

sosies.diff: Thicker leaves, net-like veins, no sour taste, burns the mouth. Poisonous.

usages: A few leaves in salad or soup.
Not advised in quantity (kidney stones, gout).

plantain.resume: Everywhere in meadows and paths. Traditionally used by crushing a leaf on a nettle or insect sting.
identification: Rosette of long, narrow leaves with 3 to 5 very marked parallel veins
Dense brown spikes on long bare stalks
usages: Young leaves in salad or cooked.
Young spikes: taste of mushroom once pan-fried.

cresson.resume: Grows in clear streams. Raw, it can transmit liver fluke (a parasite) near pastures.
identification: Hollow stems floating or creeping in running water
Compound leaves with rounded leaflets, peppery taste
Small white four-petalled flowers

sosies.diff: Toothed leaves, flowers in umbels. The umbellifer family includes deadly species by the water.

usages: Cooked only (soup), never raw if it comes from a wild stream.

tilleul.resume: Tender young leaves and flowers for tea.
identification: Large tree with asymmetric, heart-shaped, toothed leaves
Fragrant cream flowers hanging beneath a strap-shaped bract
usages: Young leaves in salad.
Dried flowers as a tea.

pin.resume: Fresh needles make a tea rich in vitamin C. The only real danger: mistaking it for yew.
identification: Needles in PAIRS, joined at the base in a small sheath
Orange bark at the top of the trunk
Small cones (pine cones)

sosies.diff: Flat needles, single, one by one, dark green, no resin smell. Deadly.
Single but prickly needles, square in cross-section. Young May shoots are edible.

usages: Steep a handful of chopped needles for 10 minutes in hot (not boiling) water.
Avoid during pregnancy.

bardane.resume: Its clinging burrs inspired Velcro. The first-year root is eaten cooked.
identification: Very large heart-shaped leaves, white woolly underside
Round fruits covered with hooks that cling to clothing
Long taproot

sosies.diff: Smaller leaves, downy on top, without a white underside. Deadly.
Poisonous leaves, red stalk. Don't confuse them in the garden.

usages: Root peeled, cut and boiled or sautéed.
Dig only with the owner's permission.

pomme.resume: Small, very sour apples, best cooked.
identification: Small tree, sometimes thorny
Small apples 2 to 4 cm, green to yellow
usages: Cooked as a compote or on the fire.
Don't crunch the pips in quantity.

merisier.resume: Small sweet cherries at forest edges, often raided by birds.
identification: Large tree with smooth red-brown bark that peels in horizontal strips
Red to black cherries on long stalks

sosies.diff: Hedge shrub with thick, shiny evergreen leaves, fruit in upright clusters. Poisonous.

usages: Raw. Don't crunch the stones.

chenopode.resume: A weed of disturbed ground, the wild cousin of spinach.
identification: Diamond-shaped, toothed leaves, covered with a white, mealy powder (especially underneath and at the top)
Small green flowers in clusters
usages: Cooked like spinach.
Avoid treated crops and field edges.

mauve.resume: Mild, slightly mucilaginous leaves and flowers.
identification: Rounded leaves with 5 to 7 shallow lobes
Large pink-mauve flowers streaked with dark veins
usages: Flowers raw in salad, leaves cooked in soup.

lierreterrestre.resume: A small, very fragrant creeping plant, used like an aromatic herb.
identification: Creeping square stems
Round, kidney-shaped, scalloped, opposite leaves
Violet tubular flowers in spring

sosies.diff: Woody climbing plant with leathery, shiny leaves. Poisonous.

usages: In small amounts to flavour a salad or an omelette.

muguet.resume: Deadly look-alike of wild garlic, growing in the same woodland.
identification: 2 to 3 leaves wrapped around each other at the base of the same stalk
Fragrant white bells in a one-sided cluster
Red berries in summer
usages: Eat nothing.

colchique.resume: Its spring leaves are confused with wild garlic. Mauve flowers in autumn, without leaves.
identification: In spring: large leaves in a tight tuft coming from the same point, with a capsule in the centre
In autumn: mauve tulip-like flowers sitting on the ground
usages: Eat nothing.

arum.resume: Common in damp woodland. Burns the mouth and throat, red berries attractive to children.
identification: Arrow-shaped leaves, net-like veins, sometimes spotted with black
Pale green hood-shaped flower around a purple finger
Spike of bright red berries in summer
usages: Eat nothing.

belladone.resume: Forest clearings and chalky edges. A few berries can kill a child.
identification: Bushy plant up to 1.5 m
Brown-purple bell-shaped flowers
Shiny black berry like a cherry, sitting on a five-pointed green star

sosies.diff: A small shrub at ground level, matt blue berries with a crown. Deadly nightshade is a tall plant.

usages: Eat nothing.

cigue.resume: The most famous umbellifer. Waste ground, path edges and ditches.
identification: Tall, smooth stem spotted with purple, hairless
Very finely divided leaves like parsley
Unpleasant mousy smell when crushed

sosies.diff: Absolute rule: no wild umbellifer is eaten without an expert.

usages: Eat nothing. Wash your hands after contact.

berce.resume: A giant invasive plant along waterways. Its sap + sunlight cause severe burns and lasting scars.
identification: Giant 2 to 4 m tall, thick stem spotted with purple
Huge, deeply divided leaves
White umbels 50 cm across
usages: Don't touch. If contact: wash with soap and water, cover the skin and keep it out of the sun for 48 h, see a doctor if blisters appear.

aconit.resume: One of the most poisonous plants in Europe, even through prolonged touch. Damp meadows and stream banks.
identification: Leaves deeply cut into strips
Blue-violet helmet-shaped flowers (June–August)
usages: Don't pick, don't handle with bare hands.

houx.resume: Its red winter berries cause vomiting and diarrhoea.
identification: Shrub with shiny, prickly evergreen leaves
Bright red berries in winter
usages: Eat nothing.

fusain.resume: Bright pink “bishop's hat” fruits, very decorative and poisonous.
identification: Green twigs with 4 corky angles
Pink four-lobed capsules opening on orange seeds
usages: Eat nothing.

bryone.resume: A hedgerow climber with red berries and a large root (“devil's turnip”).
identification: Climbing vine with spring-like tendrils
Five-lobed, rough leaves
Small red berries in clusters
usages: Eat nothing.
